title: Should We Rebuild What Time Has Taken?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In the decades since the end of the twentieth century, the impulse to rebuild what war, fire or neglect has destroyed has grown conspicuously stronger. Bridges, temples, libraries and entire town centres have been recreated, frequently with great technical ingenuity and almost invariably to public acclaim. The impulse is not new, but it has been made far more attractive by digital survey techniques, which allow lost structures to be modelled from fragments of evidence with an apparent exactness that earlier generations of restorers could only have envied. It would be tempting to regard this development as straightforwardly benign, since few people mourn the absence of a ruin. I wish to suggest, however, that the enthusiasm for reconstruction is more problematic than it appears, and that it deserves rather more scepticism than it commonly receives.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The arguments in favour are weighty and ought to be stated fairly. A community that has lost a building at the heart of its identity may experience the gap as a continuing injury, and rebuilding can be an act of collective recovery, a way of declaring that the violence did not succeed in erasing a shared past. There are economic arguments too: reconstructed monuments attract visitors, sustain skilled trades and provide employment in places that have little else to offer. Defenders add that traditional crafts, such as stone carving and timber framing, survive only when they are practised on ambitious commissions, so that a rebuilt cathedral may serve as an apprenticeship for an entire generation. I do not wish to dismiss any of these considerations, which seem to me entirely sincere. My doubt is whether they establish what their proponents believe they establish.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The first difficulty concerns authenticity, a word so overworked that its meaning has become blurred. Conservation charters adopted in the middle of the last century insisted that the value of a historic structure resides substantially in its original material, which carries the marks of its making and the traces of every subsequent use. A reconstruction, however faithful in outline, contains none of that evidence. It is a new building that happens to borrow the name, and often the silhouette, of an old one. This distinction may seem pedantic to visitors who cannot tell the difference, but it matters because the pleasure we take in a historic object arguably depends upon our belief that it is what it claims to be. Once that belief is disturbed, the experience is not so much deepened as quietly counterfeited.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A second difficulty is that reconstruction compels its sponsors to decide which moment in a building's past to restore. Most significant structures have been altered repeatedly: a church may have acquired a new tower in one century, lost a chapel in another and received an entirely different interior in a third. To rebuild it is to select one of these phases as the true building and, implicitly, to discard the rest. The choice is rarely innocent. It tends to favour whichever period is thought most glorious or most conveniently national, and the long accumulation of change that made the building interesting is flattened into a single, tidy image. A ruin, by contrast, preserves the record of its history without presuming to resolve it, and invites visitors to reconstruct the past in their own imagination.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Third, there is the matter of resources. Money devoted to a spectacular rebuilding is money withheld from the unglamorous maintenance of surviving buildings, whose condition is often precarious precisely because repairing roofs and drains attracts neither donors nor headlines. Reconstruction projects also tend to be politically convenient. Governments seeking to assert continuity with a favoured past have understood that a rebuilt monument can be presented as proof of unbroken tradition, and critics have noted instances in which the choice of what to rebuild, and what to leave in rubble, reflected the preferences of those in power rather than the wishes of the community. The economic benefits mentioned earlier may therefore be real without being sufficient; a justification that would equally support a theme park cannot, I think, be the whole case for restoring a cathedral.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Defenders of reconstruction have an effective rejoinder, which is that the ruin is itself a construction. The picturesque fragment admired by Romantic travellers was the accidental product of neglect, pillage and weather, and the habit of preferring it to the intact original is a matter of taste rather than principle. I accept the force of this observation. What follows instead is a case for restraint and for honesty: interventions should be limited to what the surviving evidence can genuinely support, made from materials that are clearly distinguishable from the old fabric, and designed so that they could be removed by later generations who judge differently. Digital models, which cost nothing in stone and can be revised at will, may in many cases offer a more truthful kind of recovery than any physical rebuilding.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this amounts to a prohibition. There will be rare cases, perhaps where a building's function was inseparable from its form and the community's need is acute, in which full reconstruction is the least bad option. But these should be treated as exceptions requiring argument, rather than as a default to be assumed whenever funds and technology permit. The deeper question is not whether a building can be rebuilt but what we hope the rebuilding will accomplish, and whether those hopes can be met by objects that are, in the last analysis, convincing copies. If the answer is that we wish to remember, then the evidence of loss may serve memory better than its concealment; if it is that we wish to forget, we should at least be candid about what we are choosing.
